scenarios.title: Scenario 3 — Multi-Agent Research System
scenarios.domains: D1 Agentic Architecture · D2 Tool Design & MCP · D5 Context & Reliability
scenarios.brief: A public-policy think tank runs a research system on the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent decomposes each analyst request and delegates through the Task tool to a web-search subagent, a document-analysis subagent that reads PDFs from a licensed journal database and other archives exposed over MCP, a synthesis subagent and a report subagent. Briefings go to legislative staff and must cite every claim to a document and page.

scenarios.title: Scenario 4 — Developer Productivity with Claude
scenarios.domains: D1 Agentic Architecture · D2 Tool Design & MCP · D3 Claude Code Configuration
scenarios.brief: A food-delivery company's platform team uses Claude Code in a 900k-line monorepo: Kotlin backend services, a TypeScript web app and shared protobuf contracts. Engineers use the built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) to explore and change code, plus MCP servers for the company's feature-flag service and its design-docs wiki. A few engineers also script Claude through the Agent SDK.

questions.question: The coordinator split a briefing on a state water-rights reform into three strands: legislative history, farm impact and municipal supply. Each subagent did its strand well. But the briefing missed a federal court ruling that changes how the reform applies. The ruling was mentioned only in footnotes of PDFs the analysis subagent had already read. Nothing in the request or in public coverage pointed to it. An earlier housing briefing missed a key settlement the same way. What is the most effective change?

options.t: Revise the coordinator's planning instructions so reform requests also get a court-rulings strand alongside the legislative and economic ones.
options.why: Runner-up. Broadening the decomposition is right when the missing areas are foreseeable from the request. These items surfaced only inside documents already retrieved, so no up-front split would have named them, and the next miss will be something else.

options.t: Include the complete findings returned by earlier subagents in each later subagent's prompt, alongside its own assignment and its quality criteria.
options.why: Incorrect. Passing prior findings explicitly is good practice for dependent subagents, but nothing here assigns anyone to investigate what those findings depend on.

options.t: Have the coordinator examine each draft for premises its evidence leans on but nobody investigated, commission follow-up work on those, and redraft.
options.why: Correct. An iterative refinement loop (evaluate the synthesis for gaps, re-delegate, re-synthesize) catches gaps that only become visible in intermediate findings.

options.t: Give the synthesis subagent a scoped lookup tool for quick factual checks while drafting, with deeper questions still routed through the coordinator.
options.why: Incorrect. A scoped cross-role tool suits frequent simple verifications; researching a federal ruling and a compact amendment is substantive work that belongs to the coordinator's delegation.

questions.decider: The ruling surfaced only inside documents already read, and the same kind of miss happened on another topic, so no up-front plan could have named it; if such gaps were predictable from the request, broadening the decomposition would win.
questions.explanation: Decomposition covers only what is knowable at the start. When gaps emerge from what subagents find, the coordinator should evaluate the synthesis for gaps, re-delegate targeted work and re-synthesize.

eli5.question: A report went out with a hole in it. The question asks how to stop holes like this. The clue is: the ruling appeared only in footnotes of documents already read, and nothing in the request pointed to it.
eli5.answer: Think of a school project where the team splits the topic before anyone has read anything. Some important things only show up once you start reading. So someone has to read the draft, spot what it leans on but never checked, and send people back to research it (an iterative refinement loop: check the synthesis for gaps, re-delegate, re-synthesize). Adding more topics to the plan up front can't catch things nobody could know about at the start. Rule: if a gap can only be seen after reading, fix it with a check-and-redo loop, not a bigger plan.
options: Runner-up. Adding court and treaty topics to the plan (fixing the task decomposition) would win if gaps were predictable from the type of request. Here they hide in footnotes and differ from topic to topic.
Handing each helper the earlier helpers' notes (explicit context passing) is good practice. But nobody is told to chase what those notes depend on, so the hole stays.
Correct. The coordinator reviews the draft, finds what is missing, sends researchers back, and rewrites.
A quick fact-check tool for the writer (a scoped cross-role tool) suits small, frequent checks. Researching a court ruling is real research, and that belongs to the coordinator.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a gap in the report means the coordinator planned the work too narrowly. Sometimes it does. But a plan can only name what is knowable when the request arrives. When the missing material sits inside documents the team had already read, no better plan would have named it in advance. The fix has to come after the reading: someone checks the draft for what it leans on and sends researchers back.

                      +-- re-delegate+

questions.question: The document-analysis subagent often finds PDFs whose key tables come from datasets it cannot open. It reports each case to the coordinator, and each round trip adds delay. An engineer proposes a shared board where subagents post such requests for the web-search subagent. The right follow-up varies by case: a search for a public copy, a narrower claim, or a question to the analyst. The choice depends on what other subagents have already found. Which design best fits?

options.t: Keep each unopened-dataset case flowing to the coordinator as a typed field in the analysis return, and leave the choice of follow-ups with it.
options.why: Correct. Hub-and-spoke: the coordinator sees every subagent's results, so it is the only place that can choose correctly among searching, narrowing or asking the analyst.

options.t: Create the shared request board, have the web-search subagent watch it for new items, and let the coordinator read the board when it aggregates.
options.why: Incorrect. Subagents have isolated context by design; a shared board lets them act around the coordinator, which then cannot pick the right follow-up or own failures.

options.t: Give the analysis subagent a scoped tool that searches for a public copy of a cited dataset, with other follow-ups still sent to the coordinator.
options.why: Runner-up. A limited cross-role tool is right for a frequent, uniform need. Here a search is only one of several follow-ups, and whether it is right depends on other subagents' findings that the analysis subagent cannot see.

options.t: Start the web-search subagent alongside the analysis subagent by emitting both Task calls in one coordinator response at the outset.
options.why: Incorrect. Parallel spawning helps independent work; the search here cannot be specified until the analysis subagent has found the missing dataset.

questions.decider: The right follow-up varies and depends on what other subagents found, which only the coordinator sees; if the follow-up were nearly always the same simple search, the scoped cross-role tool would win.
questions.explanation: In a coordinator-subagent design, inter-subagent requests flow through the coordinator, which sees all results and decides routing. Scoped cross-role tools are the exception for high-frequency, simple needs.

eli5.question: One helper keeps hitting data it can't open. Who should decide what happens next? The clue is: the right follow-up varies, and it depends on what other helpers have already found.
eli5.answer: Picture a restaurant kitchen. A cook runs out of an ingredient and tells the head chef. Only the head chef knows what every station is making, so only they can choose to buy more, change the dish, or ask the customer. In an agent system that head chef is the coordinator (the hub in hub-and-spoke), and helpers keep separate memories (isolated context). So the helper reports the problem in a clear, labelled form, and the coordinator decides. Rule: when the next step depends on everyone's work, route it through the coordinator.
options: Correct. The helper reports the problem in a labelled field, and the coordinator, who sees everything, picks the follow-up.
A shared noticeboard lets helpers act behind the head chef's back (no isolated context, no central error handling). The coordinator can no longer pick the right follow-up.
Runner-up. A small search tool for the helper (a scoped cross-role tool) wins when the need is frequent and always the same. Here a search is right only about a third of the time.
Starting both helpers at once (parallel Task calls) suits independent jobs. The search can't be written until the analysis helper finds what's missing.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the round-trip delay is the problem to solve. It is a cost, but not the deciding fact. What matters is who can make the follow-up decision. If the right next step depends on what several helpers found, only the coordinator, the one agent that sees every result, can choose it. Subagents have isolated context: they don't see each other's work.

questions.question: For energy-subsidy briefings, the coordinator emits four Task calls in one response: legislative search, regulatory review, cost-data search and stakeholder search. The regulatory reviewer must examine the rules issued under the statutes in scope. Which statutes are in scope is known only after the legislative search returns. Today the reviewer's output is generic and often covers the wrong statutes. The other three subagents work well. Which change should the team make?

options.t: Keep the four parallel Task calls and expand the regulatory prompt with the topic's jurisdiction, date range, expected output format and quality criteria.
options.why: Runner-up. Richer explicit context is the fix when a subagent's input is independent of the others. Its key input, the statute list, does not exist until the legislative search finishes.

options.t: Add a refinement step where the coordinator checks the regulatory output against the final statute list and re-delegates any mismatched sections.
options.why: Incorrect. A gap-and-refine loop is useful for discoveries made late; here the dependency is known in advance, so re-doing half the work each run is avoidable.

options.t: Restrict the regulatory reviewer's tools to the regulations database, removing general web search from its AgentDefinition tool list.
options.why: Incorrect. Scoping tools to role is good practice, but the reviewer drifts because it does not know which statutes matter, not because of the tools it holds.

options.t: Hold the regulatory Task until the statute list is back, include that list in its prompt, and run the other two searches in parallel.
options.why: Correct. A dependent subtask waits for its input, which is passed explicitly in its prompt; independent subtasks still run in parallel via multiple Task calls.

questions.decider: The reviewer needs the legislative search's output before it can start; if its work did not depend on another subagent's results, keeping it parallel with a richer prompt would be right.
questions.explanation: Subagents receive only what is in their prompt. Spawn independent work in parallel, but sequence a subtask after the one whose findings it needs and include those findings in full.

eli5.question: One of four helpers produces vague, off-target work. The question asks what to change. The clue is: which statutes are in scope is known only after the legislative search returns.
eli5.answer: Think of baking: you can't ice a cake that hasn't been baked yet. The rules reviewer needs the list of laws, and that list only exists after the legislative search finishes. So run the search first, hand its full results to the reviewer in its instructions, and let the two unrelated searches run at the same time. Helpers only know what you put in their prompt (no shared memory). Rule: run independent jobs in parallel, but make a job wait for the results it depends on, and pass them in full.
options: Runner-up. A richer prompt (more explicit context) would win if the reviewer's job didn't depend on another helper's results. Here the key input doesn't exist yet when it starts.
A check-and-redo pass (a refinement loop) is for surprises found later. This dependency is known in advance, so redoing half the work every run is wasteful.
Limiting a helper's tools (tool scoping) is good hygiene. But the reviewer drifts because it doesn't know which laws matter, not because of its tools.
Correct. Wait for the law list, pass it in full, and keep the other two searches parallel.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think vague output means a vague prompt, so you add more detail. That works when the subagent already has what it needs. Here its key input, the list of statutes, does not exist yet when it starts, because all four tasks start at once. No amount of prompt detail can supply information that hasn't been produced.

questions.question: Analysts complain that every request takes several minutes. Most requests are narrow factual questions, such as the effective date of one regulation. For those, the coordinator still runs search, document analysis, synthesis and report in sequence. The synthesis and report stages take most of the time and change the answer little. Subagents rarely fetch the same documents. Briefings for complex requests are rated well. Which change best addresses the complaint?

options.t: Send the synthesis and report stages through the Message Batches API and notify each analyst by email when their answer is ready.
options.why: Incorrect. Batch processing trades latency for cost, with up to a 24-hour window; it makes interactive answers slower.

options.t: Let the coordinator judge how much of the pipeline each request warrants and skip the drafting stages for narrow questions.
options.why: Correct. The coordinator should select subagents by query complexity rather than always running the full pipeline; that removes the slow stages from most requests.

options.t: Partition sources between the search and analysis subagents, assigning each PDF to one subagent and passing its content to the other on request.
options.why: Runner-up. Partitioning scope is right when duplicated work drives the delay. Here subagents rarely fetch the same documents; the time goes on stages that narrow questions do not need.

options.t: Emit the search and analysis Task calls in one coordinator response, running both subagents in parallel instead of one after the other.
options.why: Incorrect. Parallel Task calls suit independent work; analysis depends on what search finds, and the bulk of the time is in later stages.

questions.decider: Most requests are narrow and spend most of their time in stages they do not need, while subagents rarely duplicate work; if duplicated fetching were the main cost, scope partitioning would win.
questions.explanation: A coordinator should choose which subagents to invoke based on the request, not route everything through the full pipeline.

eli5.question: Every request takes minutes, and people are annoyed. The question asks what fixes the wait. The clue is: most requests are narrow questions, and the slow stages barely change their answers.
eli5.answer: Imagine a library where asking 'what time do you close?' gets you a full written report. Most questions need a quick answer, not the whole process. The coordinator should look at each request and call only the helpers it needs (dynamic subagent selection). That removes the slow stages from most requests. Rule: match the size of the pipeline to the size of the question.
options: The batch service (Message Batches API) is cheaper but can take up to 24 hours. That makes waiting worse, not better.
Correct. Small questions skip the slow writing stages.
Runner-up. Splitting who fetches what (scope partitioning) would win if duplicate work were the main cost. Here helpers rarely overlap, so there is little to save.
Running both helpers at once (parallel Task calls) only helps independent work. Analysis needs search's results, and the slow part comes later anyway.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a slow multi-agent system needs better division of work between its helpers, such as splitting sources so nobody fetches twice. That helps when helpers overlap. But here the time goes on whole stages that most requests don't need. The real issue is that every request runs the full pipeline, whatever its size.

questions.obj: 1.7 Resume vs fresh session with summary
questions.question: A research session on rail-freight policy was paused on Friday. By then the analysis subagent had read dozens of journal articles. Over the weekend, the publisher replaced most of those articles with corrected editions. Several tables the coordinator had quoted have changed. The session history still holds the original tool results. On Monday the analyst wants to continue and add two new questions. What is the most reliable way to continue?

options.t: Resume with --resume rail-freight, tell the agent which articles now have corrected editions, and add the two new questions.
options.why: Runner-up. Resuming and informing the agent of changes is right when a few sources changed. With most results superseded, the history is dominated by stale tables the model may keep reasoning from.

options.t: Resume with --resume rail-freight, run /compact to reduce context usage, then re-read the corrected editions within that session.
options.why: Incorrect. /compact reduces context usage but summarizes the stale results rather than removing them, so superseded figures can survive in the summary.

options.t: Open a fresh session from a structured digest of the findings that still hold, with the corrected editions queued for re-reading.
options.why: Correct. When much of the prior tool output is stale, a new session with a structured summary is more reliable than resuming over outdated results.

options.t: Use fork_session to branch the Friday session into one line of work for the original questions and one for the new questions.
options.why: Incorrect. Forking suits divergent approaches from a valid baseline; both branches would inherit the same stale tool results.

questions.decider: Most of the articles were replaced, so most tool results in the history are stale; if only one or two had changed, resuming and telling the agent about them would win.
questions.explanation: Resume when prior context is still mostly valid and tell the agent what changed; start fresh with a structured summary when much of the history is stale.

eli5.question: A paused research session needs to continue after the weekend. The question asks the most reliable way. The clue is: the publisher replaced most of the articles the session had already read.
eli5.answer: Picture a notebook full of figures copied from textbooks, and then most of the textbooks get reprinted with corrections. Writing 'some pages changed' on the cover doesn't stop you reading the old numbers. It is safer to start a fresh notebook with a clean summary of what is still true, and re-read the new editions (a new session seeded with a structured summary). Resuming (--resume) keeps all the old tool results in memory. Rule: resume when little changed; start fresh with a summary when much of the history is stale.
options: Runner-up. Resuming and listing what changed is right when only a few sources changed. With most articles replaced, the old tables still dominate what the model reads.
Squashing the history (/compact) shrinks it, but it summarizes the stale figures rather than removing them.
Correct. A fresh start with a summary of what still holds, plus re-reading the corrected editions.
Branching (fork_session) is for trying two approaches from a good starting point. Both branches would carry the same stale data.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think resuming is always the most faithful way to continue, because it keeps everything. But 'everything' includes old tool results. If most of them are now wrong, the model keeps reading wrong tables even after you tell it what changed. Past a certain point, a clean summary of what is still true beats a full history of what used to be true.

questions.question: Three vendor-hosted MCP servers feed the document-analysis subagent. Each reports publication dates in a different format: Unix timestamps, quarter strings like 'Q3 2024', and day-first dates. The synthesis subagent sometimes puts events in the wrong order. The servers are run by the vendors, and the team cannot change their responses. What is the best fix?

options.t: Register a PostToolUse hook on the team's agent that rewrites every publication date in those results to one format before the model reads them.
options.why: Correct. A PostToolUse hook normalizes heterogeneous formats deterministically before the model reasons over them, on the side of the boundary the team controls.

options.t: Change the three servers' responses to emit ISO 8601 dates, with an explicit precision field for quarter-only values such as 'Q3 2024'.
options.why: Runner-up. Fixing formats at the source is cleanest when the team runs the servers. These are vendor-hosted endpoints, so their responses are not the team's to change.

options.t: Add few-shot examples to the analysis subagent's prompt showing each vendor's date format converted to ISO 8601, one example per server.
options.why: Incorrect. Few-shot examples improve consistency but remain probabilistic, and day-first and month-first dates cannot be told apart reliably by reading.

options.t: Require the synthesis output to show each source's publication date beside every claim drawn from it, in the reader-facing briefing.
options.why: Incorrect. Showing publication dates helps readers interpret temporal differences, but the dates shown would still be mis-parsed upstream.

questions.decider: The team cannot change the vendors' server responses; if the team ran the servers, fixing the dates in the servers' own output would be the better fix.
questions.explanation: PostToolUse hooks intercept tool results and normalize them before the model sees them, giving deterministic behaviour where prompts give only probabilistic compliance.

eli5.question: Three outside services write dates in different ways, and the system gets the order of events wrong. The question asks for the best fix. The clue is: the team cannot change the servers' responses.
eli5.answer: Think of parcels arriving from three countries with labels in different formats. You can't change how other countries label parcels. But you can put a sorting desk at your own door that relabels every parcel in one standard way before anyone handles it (a PostToolUse hook, which rewrites tool results before the model sees them). It's code, so it works every time, unlike instructions in a prompt. Rule: if you can't fix the source, normalize at your own door with a hook.
options: Correct. A hook on your side rewrites every date into one format before the model reads it.
Runner-up. Fixing the dates at the source would win if your team ran those servers. They belong to the vendors, so you can't change them.
Worked examples in the prompt (few-shot) help but are still guesses. And 03/04 vs 04/03 can't be told apart by the model reliably.
Showing dates next to claims helps readers, but the dates would already be misread before they get there.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the cleanest fix is always at the source: make the servers send proper dates. That is true when you own the servers. But a fix you can't make is not a fix. When the data comes from someone else's service, the right place is the first point you control: the moment the result arrives in your agent, before the model reads it.

questions.question: The archive search tool's wrapper catches connection errors and returns an empty list instead. The archive's index goes offline for a rebuild every night, for up to two hours. Analysts submit requests at any hour. The coordinator treats an empty list as a search that ran and found nothing. As a result, one briefing wrongly stated that no committee testimony existed. options.why: Runner-up. Local retry is right for brief transient faults. A rebuild of up to two hours outlasts it, after which the outage still looks identical to a genuine no-match.

options.why: Correct. Distinguishing an access failure from a valid empty result, with structured category and retryability, lets the coordinator wait, reroute or flag the gap.

options.t: Fall back to the web-search subagent whenever the archive returns nothing, letting the coordinator merge whatever public sources it finds.
options.why: Incorrect. Committee testimony may not be public, and the coordinator still cannot tell an outage from a real absence in the archive.

options.t: Record the query, timestamp and hit count of each archive call in the claim-source metadata that the coordinator passes to synthesis.
options.why: Incorrect. Provenance metadata is useful, but a hit count of zero still does not say whether the search ran.

questions.decider: The outage lasts up to two hours, and the coordinator cannot tell it from a real no-match; if failures were brief blips, local retry with backoff would be the first fix.
questions.explanation: Tools must distinguish access failures from valid empty results and return structured error metadata (isError, category, retryability) so the agent can recover appropriately.

eli5.question: A search said 'nothing found' when the archive was actually down. The question asks how the tool should behave. The clue is: the outage can last up to two hours, and the coordinator reads an empty list as 'searched, found nothing'.
eli5.answer: Imagine phoning a shop and getting no answer, then telling your boss 'they don't sell it'. 'Closed' and 'doesn't have it' are different answers. The tool must say 'I couldn't search, try later' as a real error (isError with a category and a retryable flag). A genuine empty result stays a normal answer (a valid empty result). Then the coordinator can wait, reroute, or flag the gap. Rule: never let 'couldn't look' look the same as 'looked and found nothing'.
options: Runner-up. Retrying a few times (local retry with backoff) is right for brief blips. A two-hour rebuild outlasts it, and the failure still ends up looking like 'nothing found'.
Correct. Report the outage as a labelled, retryable failure and keep real empty results as normal answers.
Asking the web instead might help, but committee testimony may not be public. And the coordinator still can't tell 'down' from 'none'.
Logging the query and hit count is useful record-keeping (provenance). But zero hits still doesn't say whether the search actually ran.

deep.premise: It is tempting to see a connection error and reach for retries. Retrying is right for brief blips. But the real damage here is not the failure. It is that the failure looked exactly like a successful search with no results. Even a perfect retry policy ends, eventually, by returning that same misleading empty list.

eli5.question: An engineer must build a payout export in an area they don't know well. How should they start with Claude? The clue is: the old spreadsheet got some cases wrong, and nobody has decided the tricky rules.
eli5.answer: Think of a new tailor making a suit when the customer hasn't chosen the cloth or the cut. You don't copy an old suit that's known to fit badly. You ask questions first. Have Claude interview you about unusual cases (the interview pattern), then take the questions you can't answer to finance. Examples and tests come later, once the right answers are known. Rule: when the rules are unclear, have Claude ask questions before building.
options: Runner-up. Real examples of input and expected output (concrete examples) are the best guide once you trust them. These rows come from a spreadsheet known to be wrong.
Writing tests first (test-driven iteration) works when you know what 'right' looks like. These tests would only check the layout, not the unsettled rules.
Designing first (plan mode) would make Claude invent business rules nobody has set.
Correct. Claude asks about edge cases first, and the open questions go to the people who decide.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think real examples are always the best way to explain what you want. They are, when the examples are right. Here the examples come from a spreadsheet known to be wrong in unnamed cases, and the hard rules haven't been decided. Copying them would copy the mistakes. The first job is to find out what you don't know.
